notes.meaning: Jesus finished His teaching in Galilee and left that region for the last time before His death. He traveled south toward Judea by taking the route through Perea, on the east side of the Jordan River. He did not move on until His work in Galilee was fully completed.

Large crowds followed Jesus on His journey, and He healed the sick among them. Wherever Jesus went, people gathered to receive His help, and He was just as ready to heal here as He had been in Galilee. He cared for their needs even while traveling.

Some Pharisees approached Jesus with a trap, asking if a man could divorce his wife for any reason at all. Jewish teachers at that time were fiercely divided between a strict rule and a loose rule that allowed divorce over minor complaints. The questioners hoped Jesus would say something that would turn people against Him or get Him into trouble with the rulers.

Instead of taking sides in human debates, Jesus pointed them back to the creation story in Scripture. He reminded them that from the beginning, God made humanity as male and female. By creating one man and one woman, God showed His original design for marriage.

Jesus quoted Genesis to explain that a husband must leave his parents and be joined closely to his wife. The two are united so firmly that they become one flesh. This bond between husband and wife was created by God to be even closer than the bond between parents and children.

Because marriage unites two people into one flesh, they are no longer separate individuals in God's eyes. Jesus concluded that human beings have no right to break apart what God has joined together. Marriage is a sacred union made by God, not just a temporary human agreement.

The Pharisees objected by asking why Moses commanded a husband to give a wife a certificate of divorce and send her away. They treated the law of Moses as if it ordered divorce. They used this point to make Jesus appear as though He were opposing the ancient law of God.

Jesus answered that Moses did not command divorce, but only permitted it because the people had hard, stubborn hearts. This civil allowance was meant to protect wives from cruel mistreatment, not to approve of broken homes. From the beginning of creation, God never intended marriage to end in divorce.

Jesus declared that anyone who divorces his wife, except for sexual immorality, and marries another woman commits adultery. Marital unfaithfulness breaks the one-flesh bond, making it the only cause Jesus gives here for divorce. Any other breakup leaves the original marriage bond standing in God's sight.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Catholic teaching holds that a valid, consummated marriage can never be dissolved, so Jesus' exception allows a husband and wife to live apart in cases of unfaithfulness, but never permits either person to remarry while the other is alive.

other.label: Orthodox
other.view: Orthodox churches permit divorce and remarriage in certain tragic circumstances, including adultery, reflecting later church traditions and imperial laws.

notes.meaning: Hearing how strict Jesus was about marriage, the disciples remarked that if a man cannot easily leave his wife, it is better not to marry at all. They still held the common idea that easy divorce was a helpful escape from an unhappy home. Their reaction showed how hard it was even for Christ's closest followers to accept God's high standard.

Jesus explained that staying unmarried is not a rule for everyone, but only for those to whom God has given that special gift. Most people are called to marriage, and no one should choose a single life out of anger or selfish comfort. A person can only live happily and purely without marriage if God grants the grace to do so.

Jesus noted three reasons why people live without marrying: some are born without the capacity for it, others are made unable by human cruelty, and some choose to stay single to serve God's kingdom without distraction. This choice is an honorable calling for those who have received the gift, but it is never forced on anyone. Those who are able to embrace this calling should use their freedom to serve God.

Parents brought their little children to Jesus so He could place His hands on them and pray for them. The disciples scolded the people and tried to turn them away, thinking small children were too unimportant to bother the Teacher. They failed to realize how deeply Jesus cares for the weakest and youngest.

Jesus told the disciples to stop hindering the children and let them come to Him. He announced that the kingdom of heaven belongs to little ones and to everyone who trusts God with simple, childlike humility. Jesus welcomes children warmly and invites all people to come to Him with open, humble hearts.

Jesus placed His hands on the children and gave them His blessing before moving on to another place. Even though His journey was urgent, He took time to show love to the little ones. His touch showed that young children are fully able to receive God's favor and care.

A wealthy young ruler ran up, knelt before Jesus, and asked what good deed he needed to do to earn eternal life. He believed eternal life was a prize to be won by performing some great work of the law. Even though he was sincere, his focus was entirely on what he could accomplish by his own power.

Jesus asked why the man questioned Him about what is good, pointing him to the truth that God alone is completely good. He then told the young man that if he wanted to earn life by his own works, he must keep all of God's commandments. Jesus said this to help the man see God's perfect standard and realize his need for divine mercy.

When the man asked which commandments Jesus meant, Jesus listed commands that guide how we treat others: do not murder, do not commit adultery, do not steal, do not lie, honor parents, and love your neighbor as yourself. These duties show whether our outward religion is backed by real love. True devotion to God always produces honest love and respect for our neighbors.

The young man answered that he had kept all these commandments since his youth, but he still asked what he was lacking. He had obeyed the outward rules of the law, yet his heart remained uneasy and unsatisfied. His question showed both his proud belief in his own goodness and an inner awareness that something vital was missing.

Jesus told him that to be complete, he must go, sell his belongings, give the money to the poor, and follow Him. Jesus was not making a universal rule for all believers, but He tested this man's heart where he was weakest. The young man claimed to love his neighbor, but his wealth was his real idol, keeping him from truly following God.

other.label: Popular modern teaching
other.view: Popular modern teaching often known as the prosperity gospel claims that God promises financial wealth to faithful believers, but traditional interpreters point out that Jesus here warns that money can be an idol and calls this man to give it away.

notes.meaning: When the young man heard what Jesus said, he walked away full of grief because he had great wealth. He wanted eternal life, but he was not willing to let go of the riches that held his heart. His sorrow showed that when forced to choose between his possessions and Jesus, he chose his money.

Jesus turned to His disciples and told them how hard it is for a rich person to enter the kingdom of heaven. Riches often make people feel safe, proud, and self-sufficient, blinding them to their deep spiritual poverty. Earthly wealth can easily become a chain that binds the heart to this world.

Jesus repeated His warning with a vivid picture, saying it is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for a rich person to enter God's kingdom. A camel was one of the largest animals known to His hearers, making the image describe something humanly impossible. Anyone who trusts in riches cannot squeeze into God's kingdom while clinging to earthly treasures.

The disciples were completely shocked by Jesus' words and asked who could ever be saved. In their culture, wealth was commonly viewed as a sure sign of God's special favor. If even the rich, who seemed to have every advantage, could hardly enter heaven, salvation seemed out of reach for anyone.

Jesus looked directly at them and explained that while saving oneself is impossible for human beings, all things are possible with God. No person, rich or poor, can change their own heart or earn a place in heaven by human effort. Only the almighty grace and power of God can rescue sinners and free their hearts from the love of the world.

Peter pointed out that he and the other disciples had left everything behind to follow Jesus, and he asked what reward they would receive. Even though their boats and nets were humble possessions, they had truly surrendered their livelihood and homes for His sake. Jesus did not rebuke Peter for asking, but lovingly addressed their hope for the future.

Jesus promised that in the future renewal of the world, when He sits on His glorious throne, the twelve apostles will sit on twelve thrones judging the twelve tribes of Israel. They had shared in His humble work and hardships, and they would share in His royal honor and authority. God never forgets the faithful service of those who follow Christ through trials.

Jesus added that anyone who gives up homes, family, or lands for His sake will receive a hundred times more in return, along with eternal life. This reward does not mean literal piles of houses, but rich spiritual blessings, new brothers and sisters in the family of God, and endless joy in heaven. Whatever a believer gives up for Christ will be repaid far beyond measure.

Jesus concluded by warning that many who are first will be last, and the last will be first. Those who seem important, privileged, or first in this world may find themselves at the very back in God's kingdom. On the other hand, humble people who gave up everything to follow Christ will receive the highest honor from God.
